Online romance scams are arguably one of the oldest cons in the digital world, yet they continue to claim new victims. A study jointly conducted by four universities has found that AI chatbots are now even more effective at running these scams than real people — a development that is deeply worrying…

Online Romance Scams

Modern online romance scams typically start on dating apps. Victims are approached by an extremely attractive profile, with the person behind it playing the role of an ardent suitor who perfectly matches the victim's preferences.

They engage victims in lengthy online conversations that often last for months. Their usual excuse for being unable to meet in person is that they are on an extended overseas trip.

Eventually, one of two scenarios unfolds: they claim to be facing an emergency requiring an immediate wire transfer to get out of trouble, or the conversation shifts to a supposedly lucrative investment opportunity, persuading the victim to put money into a bogus cryptocurrency scheme.

These scams are known as "long cons" because they rely on building trust over extended periods, often chatting with victims every day for months on end. Although this might seem like a huge time investment for the fraudsters, these operations are typically run from scam compounds in countries like Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos, staffed by extremely low-paid workers — some of whom are trafficked and forced to labour against their will.

AI vs. Humans

Wired magazine has reported on a study conducted by four universities, using ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini.

Researchers from the four universities — Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham in India, Foscari University of Venice, the University of Melbourne, and Ben Gurion University of the Negev — pitted AI chatbots directly against humans in a simulated scam process — more precisely, the lengthy trust-building conversation that precedes the final push to get targets to make a fake investment. They found that… the AI chatbots performed remarkably well, successfully impersonating humans and even outperforming the human "scammers" in the trial on certain metrics.

The test subjects, unaware of the study's true purpose, believed they were talking to a real person regardless of whether they were conversing with a human or not. The researchers measured the level of trust established using both subjective and objective methods. When finally asked to take action, such as downloading an app, only 18% of those in the "trust-building by humans" group agreed, whereas nearly half of those who had been chatting with an AI chatbot complied.

Furthermore, when the test subjects were asked to rate how much they trusted the "person" they had been chatting with, the AI bots scored significantly higher.

This Could Lead to Scams Scaling Dramatically

Perhaps the most alarming finding of the study is that replacing humans with AI chatbots could allow scam operations to massively scale up their activities. AI scam bots can engage thousands of victims simultaneously in separate conversations.

Human intervention would only be required at the final stage — when payment is demanded — to circumvent the safety guardrails built into AI systems.
